title: Thailand floods kill 31 as forecast warns of more rain and flash flooding this week
excerpt: The Interior Ministry confirmed 31 deaths from flooding since September 16, as meteorologists forecast thunderstorms and heavy rain across upper Thailand through Wednesday.
body:
• Thailand's Interior Ministry said on October 5 that the death toll from flooding across the country since September 16 has risen to 31.
  • The Thailand Meteorological Department has warned of more rain this week: thunderstorms, strong winds and heavy downpours are expected across much of upper Thailand from Monday through Wednesday, raising flash-flood risk in low-lying areas.
  • Bangkok remains disrupted — flooded streets, stranded buses and affected roads and public transport — though both airports are operating and city rail services are running.
  • What this means for you: if you are flying to or through Bangkok this week, allow extra time for the airport run, check your route before leaving, and confirm hotel transfers — the FCDO and Tourism Authority of Thailand advise travellers to verify weather and transport conditions rather than assume normal service.

Death toll rises as new storms approach

Thailand's death toll from weeks of flooding has climbed to 31, the Interior Ministry said on Monday, as the country braces for another round of storms. The floods, which have swollen rivers and inundated communities since September 16, are the worst to hit the country in years.

The fresh warning came from the Thailand Meteorological Department, which said thunderstorms, strong winds and heavy rain are expected across much of upper Thailand from Monday through Wednesday. Low-lying areas face the highest risk of flash flooding, and authorities have urged residents to stay alert.

Context & Background

The disaster has spread across dozens of provinces, with waters reaching the capital. Images from Bangkok last week showed commuters wading through flooded streets near stranded buses, and major roads were left difficult to access under standing water. Earlier reports put the number of affected provinces at 31 and the number of people impacted at nearly three million, with emergency teams working around the clock to evacuate vulnerable families and deliver relief supplies.

Thailand is no stranger to flood disasters — the 2011 floods remain the benchmark for devastation — but the current event has stretched local resources hard. Damage assessments are continuing as water levels shift, and officials say the full picture will only become clear once floodwaters recede.

Impact & Analysis

The immediate pressure falls on transport and daily life. Roads and public transport in the capital have been affected, and the coming week's forecast threatens to complicate recovery in the provinces already under water. Emergency and response services remain under strain, and authorities are monitoring weather conditions for additional risks beyond the current three-day outlook.

For the tourism sector, timing matters. The floods arrive in the run-up to Thailand's peak travel season, and the question of whether visitors should still come has dominated travel coverage. The UK's Foreign Office warns about flooding and possible travel disruption but has not advised against travel to Bangkok because of the floods. Thailand's own tourism authority says most attractions remain open and recommends checking conditions and allowing extra travel time.

Diaspora Angle

Thailand ranks among the most popular overseas destinations for Indian travellers — Bangkok, Pattaya and Phuket draw hundreds of thousands of visitors from India each year, and a large Indian expatriate community lives and works in the country. With Diwali travel season approaching, families planning trips should treat the flood forecast as a planning input, not a reason to cancel outright: flights are operating, the city rail is running, but surface transport is unreliable in flooded areas. Travel insurance, flexible hotel bookings and a buffer of extra hours around flights are the practical moves this week.

What's Next

The next 72 hours will determine whether the death toll climbs further. All eyes are on the upper provinces where the heaviest rain is forecast, and on whether Bangkok's drainage systems can cope if northern runoff combines with coastal tides. The Interior Ministry is continuing to gather casualty and damage reports from affected regions, and further updates are expected as the new storm front moves through.
